body.hook: When a new building goes up, there are drawings, change orders, inspection reports and photographs of every stage. If something goes wrong years later, the documentation shows what was done. Professionals document their process; so will you.

study.title: Design Folio
study.question: How do I show the whole story of my design?
study.passage:
Design folio checklist (written for this lesson):
Page 1, Brief and criteria: the client, need, constraints and your measurable criteria.
Page 2, Ideas: brainstorm list and annotated thumbnails, with your chosen idea starred.
Page 3, Plan: orthographic drawing with dimensions, material choice and justification, joining plan.
Page 4, Making: three to five photos of the build with captions, plus your build log.
Page 5, Testing: fair-test plan, results table, graph and conclusion.
Page 6, Iteration: problem, root cause, change and before-and-after results.
Page 7, Final product: photo, specification and appraisal against each criterion.
Tips: keep pages in chronological order; caption every image; be honest about problems.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Gather your evidence from the whole project
Organize it into the seven folio pages
Check the folio against the checklist with a partner
discussion: Which page tells your story best?
Which evidence was hardest to find?
Why include problems, not just successes?
How could someone use your folio to build your product?
study.product: Complete a seven-page design folio for your desk organizer.

body.objective: Students will be able to explore trades careers.

body.hook: Alberta needs electricians, welders, carpenters, heavy-equipment technicians and plumbers, and many of them learn while being paid. Through apprenticeship, you can earn money and a certificate at the same time, and some students start while still in high school.

study.title: Trades Explorer
study.question: What are the pathways into the trades?
study.passage:
Information (summaries written for this lesson):
How apprenticeship works: An apprentice works for an employer under a journeyperson and is paid while learning. Most of the learning (about 80%) happens on the job; the rest is technical training at a college or polytechnic, such as SAIT in Calgary or NAIT in Edmonton. Many Alberta apprenticeships take about 2 to 4 years. After passing exams, the apprentice becomes a certified journeyperson.
RAP: In Alberta's Registered Apprenticeship Program, high school students can work as apprentices, earn wages and count the hours toward both their apprenticeship and high school credits.
Red Seal: Many trades have a Red Seal endorsement, which lets a journeyperson work across Canada.
Trade profiles: Electrician (installs and repairs electrical systems), Welder (joins metal using heat), Carpenter (builds and repairs structures), Automotive service technician (maintains and repairs vehicles), Plumber (installs pipes and water systems), Cook (prepares food in commercial kitchens).
Task: Research one trade on alis.alberta.ca: what the work involves, training length, skills needed and which CTF skills connect to it.
study.source: Summaries written for this lesson; check details for each trade on alis.alberta.ca and tradesecrets.alberta.ca.

body.objective: Students will be able to present to an audience.
body.iCan: I can present to an audience.
successCriteria: I can present my product and process to an audience
I can use my design folio and test evidence
I can answer questions about my design
body.hook: In a real design firm, the final step isn't building; it's the client meeting. You stand up with your product, your folio and your evidence, and you convince people your design works. Today you present to an audience as a professional would.

vocabulary.definition: The people you are presenting to.

study.title: Client Showcase
study.question: How do I present my design like a professional?
study.passage:
Showcase format (written for this lesson):
Each team has four minutes plus two minutes of Q&A. The audience acts as the "client panel."
1. Introduce yourselves and the brief (30 seconds).
2. Show the product and its specification (45 seconds).
3. Walk through the process using your folio: ideas, plan, build, testing, iteration (2 minutes).
4. Evidence: one key graph or result (30 seconds).
5. Close: how the product meets the brief and one thing you would do with more time (15 seconds).
Q&A tips: listen to the whole question; repeat it if needed; answer honestly; if you don't know, say how you would find out.
Panel feedback form: Clear explanation (1–4), use of evidence (1–4), professional delivery (1–4), one strength, one question.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Choose one key piece of evidence to show
Answer questions and review panel feedback
discussion: What evidence best proved your design works?
Which question from the panel was hardest?
What did the panel feedback say?
How was this presentation different from your Grade 7 one?
study.product: Deliver your showcase, then write a short response to your panel feedback naming one strength and one improvement for next time.
